The pink house at 417 Royal Street was built in 1795, after the great fire, and soon passed to Don José Faurie. It later became the Banque de la Louisiane, the first bank in Louisiana, and the bank's initials, LB, still sit in the ironwork at the centre of the balcony railing.

From 1841 to 1891 the Morphy family owned it, and Paul Morphy, the chess prodigy many called the unofficial world champion, lived there until his death in 1884.

Brennan's has served here since 1956. Guests often ask how old the building is while they wait for the first course, so point them to the balcony monogram on the way out: it is the easiest way to make the history real.

Auguste Escoffier, the chef who codified French restaurant cooking in Le Guide Culinaire, organised sauces into families. The mother sauces are espagnole, velouté, béchamel, tomate and hollandaise; every other classical sauce is a daughter, built by adding to one of them.

Brennan's menus read like a lesson in the hollandaise family: plain hollandaise on the Hussarde and Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, Choron on the Sardou, Foyot on the Chateaubriand. The marchand de vin and bordelaise come from the brown side.

The guide's own advice is that the sauce usually matters more than the protein, for the guest and for the wine. Learn the sauce on each plate first and the rest of the description follows.

Marchand de vin means wine merchant. In classical French cooking it is shallots reduced in red wine with a brown stock or demi-glace. New Orleans made its own version: onion and plenty of garlic in place of the shallot, often ham and mushrooms, beef stock and red wine, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce. Antoine's made it famous in the city.

The guide's best wording is a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce; calling it a bare reduction undersells it.

On the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen it is the dark, winey half of the two sauces, under the egg. Whether tonight's sauce carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef before you promise either.

Sauce Foyot, also called sauce Valois, is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Glace de viande is brown stock reduced until it is thick and syrupy; a spoonful turns pale, sharp béarnaise tawny, deeper and more savoury.

A roux is flour cooked in fat, stirred constantly, and used to thicken and flavour a sauce or soup. French kitchens cook it white or blond for béchamel and velouté. Louisiana cooks take it much further, to peanut butter, then chocolate or mahogany brown, which gives a toasty, nutty depth; the darker it gets, the more flavour and the less thickening power it has.

A dark roux is the Creole tradition for gumbo and turtle soup, and New Orleans marchand de vin is often roux-bound too. How dark our own kitchen takes each one is a question for the chef.

At the table, a roux is part of why a gumbo or a turtle soup tastes deep rather than brothy. Questions about flour in a dish go to the kitchen.

Brown butter, beurre noisette in French, is butter cooked past melting until its milk solids toast to the colour of hazelnuts and it smells nutty and sweet. It must be stopped at that moment, often with lemon or vinegar, because a few seconds more and it burns bitter.

That nutty depth is why it appears across our menus in different forms.

On the Louisiana Crab Claws it becomes a warm brown butter vinaigrette, sharpened with acid; the spinach in the Turtle Soup is wilted in brown butter; and the financiers in the Blackberry Trifle are made with it, which is what makes them taste buttery rather than cakey.

The skin is scored in a tight crosshatch, the breast goes skin-down into a cold or moderate pan, and the fat melts out slowly as the skin crisps. Duck breast is served pink, like a steak; cooked through it turns grey and livery.

On the dinner tasting the Rohan breast comes with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts. The usual doneness is medium-rare to medium; confirm at lineup.

Cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down in open kettles until thick, with nothing taken out. Molasses is what remains after sugar has been crystallised and removed, so cane syrup is sweeter, lighter and milder, with a buttery caramel taste rather than molasses's bitter edge. Steen's of Abbeville has made it since 1910, after a freeze threatened a cane crop.

Dosage is the small dose of wine and sugar added to a sparkling wine just before the final cork, after disgorging. It balances the high acidity, and it decides the word on the label.

From driest to sweetest: Brut Nature, no sugar added; Extra Brut, up to 6 grams a litre; Brut, up to 12; then Extra Dry, 12 to 17; Sec, 17 to 32; and Demi-Sec, 32 to 50 grams, noticeably sweet. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Pommery's Nature of 1874 helped turn the world towards dry Champagne, when much of it was very sweet.

Our house Brennan's Essential is Extra Brut, very dry; most of the list is Brut; the Moët Nectar Impérial Rosé and Laurent-Perrier Harmony are Demi-Sec, for dessert.

Rosé Champagne is the only French wine allowed to be made pink by blending red and white wine. Most houses add a little still red wine, usually Pinot Noir from villages such as Bouzy or Aÿ, to the white base before the second fermentation, which gives a reliable colour and red-fruit flavour.

The other way, saignée or maceration, leaves crushed black grapes on their skins for a short time until the juice turns pink. It gives deeper colour and more structure, and is rarer.

Most of our rosés, Moët, Taittinger, Paul Bara, Chartogne-Taillet and Veuve Fourny, use the blending method. Rosé Champagne has a little more body than white, so it suits salmon, duck and the Bananas Foster.

changes.before:
Lees are the spent yeast cells left after fermentation. Leaving a wine in contact with them, instead of drawing it off, slowly changes it: the cells break down and release compounds that add a creamy texture, roundness and flavours of bread, brioche and toast.

In Champagne and every traditional method wine the lees age inside the bottle, which is where the toasty notes and fine, creamy bubbles come from; the longer, the finer. In Muscadet the wine rests on its lees in tank through the winter, sur lie, and the best for two years or more, gaining body and a savoury depth.

So when a guest asks why a Champagne tastes of brioche, the answer is the lees, not oak or added flavour.

Botrytis cinerea is a mould that, in the right weather, becomes noble rot. It needs misty, humid autumn mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The mould pierces the grape skins and the sun dries the berries, which shrivel, losing water while the sugar and acidity concentrate.

The grapes look ruined but make the most luscious sweet wines in the world, tasting of honey, apricot, candied orange, saffron and marmalade. Because the rot spreads unevenly, pickers go through the vineyard many times, taking only the affected berries.

Sauternes and Barsac, Burgenland, the Loire and the highest Prädikat levels in Germany depend on it. On our list: Yquem, Suduiraut, Climens, Gilette, Kracher, Keller and the Grgich Violetta.

A vin doux naturel, naturally sweet wine, is made by stopping fermentation partway by adding neutral grape spirit, a process called mutage. The yeast dies, so the grape's own unfermented sugar stays in the wine, and the alcohol rises to about 15 to 18 per cent. Port is made the same way.

In Roussillon, Banyuls and Rivesaltes are then aged either fresh and fruity, or oxidatively for years in old casks or glass demijohns left out in the sun, turning amber and tasting of fig, walnut, caramel and coffee.

The La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva on the dinner tasting is aged the oxidative way; the Riveyrac Rivesaltes 1975 has spent decades in old casks. Banyuls with chocolate is the classic match.

Because fermentation is cut short, the colour and tannin must be pulled from the skins fast, so the grapes are trodden by foot in shallow stone tanks called lagares or worked in modern machines that copy it.

Then the style is set by ageing. Ruby styles, including Late Bottled Vintage and Vintage Port, age briefly in large casks and keep their dark fruit; tawny styles age for years in small casks, turning amber and nutty. Our list carries every kind.

Biodynamic farming goes further, following the ideas of Rudolf Steiner from the 1920s: it treats the vineyard as a living whole, uses herbal and mineral preparations and plans work by a lunar calendar.

A bottle of Champagne holds about six atmospheres of pressure, roughly three times a car tyre, so it is opened with care, and quietly.

Chill it to 43 to 46°F. Present the label to the host. Loosen the cage but keep a thumb or a napkin over the cork from then on. Hold the bottle at about 45 degrees, pointed away from guests, grip the cork and turn the bottle, not the cork, easing it out so it leaves with a soft sigh rather than a pop.

Pour a little into each glass to let the foam settle, then top up to about two thirds, guests first and the host last. Return the bottle to the ice bucket, half ice and half water.
